nameStory: The American Snout butterfly gets its quirky name from the unusually long, beak-like projections on the front of its head called palps. These snout-like structures make it look almost like a tiny flying Pinocchio! When the butterfly closes its wings and sits still, that prominent 'snout' combined with its mottled brown coloring helps it blend in perfectly with dead leaves.
description: The American Snout is a medium-sized butterfly with a distinctive elongated 'nose' that sets it apart from all other New England butterflies. Its wings are primarily orange-brown with darker borders and white spots, while the undersides are mottled gray-brown for camouflage. This brush-footed butterfly has a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches and belongs to a unique subfamily with only one species in our region. Despite being uncommon in New England with only 79 recorded sightings, it's quite distinctive when you do spot one.

idTips.label: Elongated snout
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable long, pointed projections extending forward from the head like a bird's beak - no other New England butterfly has this feature

idTips.label: Orange-brown wings
idTips.description: Upper wings are bright orange-brown with dark borders and crisp white spots that stand out clearly against the warm background color

idTips.label: Mottled underside
idTips.description: When wings are closed, the underside appears as a patchwork of gray, brown, and tan that feels rough-textured and resembles tree bark or dead leaves

idTips.label: Angular wing shape
idTips.description: Front wings have a distinctly squared-off, angular appearance rather than the rounded shape of most butterflies

idTips.label: Erratic flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, jerky movements and frequently lands head-down on tree trunks where it becomes nearly invisible

habitat: American Snouts are most likely found in areas where hackberry trees (Celtis species) grow, as these are their only host plants. Look for them along woodland edges, in parks with mature trees, and near streams or rivers where hackberries thrive. They prefer areas with some open space for flying but close to their host trees for egg-laying.

seasonality.spring: Adults may emerge in late spring if conditions are right, but sightings are unpredictable as this species doesn't have a regular annual cycle in New England.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time when most sightings occur, with adults actively seeking mates and females laying eggs singly on hackberry leaves.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may appear in warm autumns, with fresh adults sometimes seen into October before seeking overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected spots like tree crevices or under loose bark, remaining completely inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: American Snout butterflies are famous for forming massive migrations of millions of individuals in Texas, creating clouds so thick they show up on weather radar and sometimes force cars to pull over due to poor visibility!
confusionNotes: The prominent snout makes this butterfly nearly impossible to confuse with any other species in New England. When perched with wings closed, someone might mistake it for a dead leaf or piece of bark rather than a living butterfly, but no other butterfly has those distinctive beak-like projections.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's common across America, the American Snout is actually quite rare in New England and much more abundant in southern states. The 'snout' isn't actually a nose but rather modified mouthparts called palps that help the butterfly taste and smell.
compareHints: As the only snout butterfly in New England, there are no close relatives to compare it with in our region. Among other brush-footed butterflies, it's most easily distinguished by its unique snout and the angular, rather than rounded, wing shape. The combination of orange upperwings and mottled bark-like underwings is also distinctive within the brush-footed butterfly family.
